title: Right of centre*: Searching for higher education at Reform UK’s Annual Conference

The post Right of centre*: Searching for higher education at Reform UK’s Annual Conference appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Whenever I go to a political party’s conference, I can never quite resist the temptation to see the quality of organisation as a proxy for their ability to govern. It’s incredibly unfair, especially for a party that is as new as Reform UK. But judging by the hour-long queue just to collect a pass, they still have some distance to go before they are ready for government. Perhaps one of their Tory defectors can explain the Royal Mail’s tried-and-tested method of getting conference passes to people in advance (known as the post).

Once in, it was evident the higher education sector was, perhaps surprisingly and for the first time at a Reform UK conference, out in force. I saw friends from the Russell Group, MillionPlus, University Alliance, the University of Manchester, the University of Leicester, UCL, the University of Sussex – I could go on. To my mind, it was good to see the sector engaging in this way (as proposed in a recent HEPI paper).

However, there weren’t many events specifically focused on higher education or research. So special kudos to Luke Tryl and his More in Common team, who were not only doing their bit to protect the reputation of pollsters after the latest scandal but who also hosted some excellent and well-attended events, including one on attitudes to science.

The panellists may not have seen eye-to-eye on everything, including how to talk to voters about science, but the conversation was more consensual on the need for a sensible pro-science conversation than some might have expected in advance. For me, the most memorable moment was when Baroness (Claire) Fox, a former Brexit Party MEP and now a non-affiliated peer, bemoaned the tendency to shut down important conversations with the phrase ‘the science says’, while remaining fiercely pro-science herself. Claire was also rightly keen to plug her always brilliant Battle of Ideas taking place in London in mid-October, which often hosts many lively debates on higher education.

It’s worth remembering, when searching for links between Reform UK and academia, that Nigel Farage made his name by taking over a political party (UKIP) set up by an academic (Alan Sked) and that one of Reform’s current big names is another academic (Matt Goodwin) while one of the two senior Reform UK staffers caught up in the funding sting is a Cambridge academic (James Orr).

Other parties tend not to have such a high proportion of former academics among their key personnel – even if it has encouraged rather than limited the rhetorical attacks on universities. To at least one of the hecklers during his big set-piece speech, Nigel Farage made a jibe about university education. From the 1950s on, the far-right League of Empire Loyalists, a precursor to the National Front, sought to disrupt Tory party conferences for not being right-wing enough; today, those trying to shut down political debate are seemingly more likely to hail from the left.

One thing that is the same at the Reform UK Conference as at every other party conference is the tendency of leading figures to turn up late to the sessions at which they’re speaking, as they dash from engagement to engagement. And so it was with Suella Braverman, Reform UK’s Education spokesperson, for a fringe session on ‘outcomes for disadvantaged white young men’. Once she arrived, her opening remarks attacked a long list of organisations for the educational shortfalls that exist, including the Labour Party, her former colleagues in the Conservative Party and even MI5, who she described as ‘racist’ for their internship programme.

Professor Malcolm Press, the President of Universities UK, responded on behalf of the higher education sector. He accepted the main outline of Suella’s argument: in other words, that there is a genuine problem of educational underachievement among young white men. HEPI’s output confirms this too. Malcolm also sensibly linked poor white boys’ relative disadvantage to long-term changes in the labour market.

Suella then moved on to blame the failure of so many boys not on them as individuals but rather on institutions and societal structures. That may resonate with many people (including parents), though I am not sure I expected Reform UK to sound so much like sociologists, especially given sociology is sometimes another one of Nigel Farage’s targets.

Suella’s critique led her to propose policy changes that, at a high level, seemed completely indistinguishable from Andy Burnham’s and Lucy Powell’s policies and, for that matter, those of the Conservatives: more apprenticeships and the like. Anyone playing word bingo would have done well, with ‘parity of esteem’, ‘Germany and Switzerland’ and more ‘vocational education’ raising their heads.

To me, it seemed a little same-y for an insurgent party seeking to offer a brave new world. Did Suella really break her bonds with her original party because she was desperate to match their commitments on tertiary education? Perhaps not, as we were told in Farage’s big speech that she would be saying a whole lot more about higher education on Saturday afternoon.

Intriguingly, and I don’t think this is just my wishful thinking, Farage’s hint that university places would be strictly controlled in future didn’t seem to go down quite as well in the hall as his other commitments – perhaps even Reform UK activists are coming to see tight student number caps might shut their children and grandchildren out of higher education? (I say ‘children and grandchildren’ because, while Students for Reform did have a small stand and were hosting an event, the most common demographic at the conference was older men.)

Suella Braverman went on in the same fringe session, after some prompting from the Chair, to blame a lot of the existing challenges faced by young white men on EDI / DEI initiatives. In his usual emollient and persuasive way, Malcolm responded with an agenda that was actually much more radically different than many people in the room may have realised, for he made the clear practical case for privately-funded bursaries and scholarships limited to specific groups that have been under-represented in higher education. This won a rare round of applause from the Reform activists in the room. Given the focus of the event was on poor white men, they loved the idea of targeted support. Perhaps they didn’t spot the contradiction between Suella’s critique of EDI schemes and Malcolm’s call for more support targeted at specific groups. But in the end, a targeted bursary is a form of EDI.

The most memorable moments of the conference overall were those remembering Ann Widdecombe. I felt I had come full circle as the first ever party conference I attended was the Tory one of 2000, where Ann Widdecombe’s promised crackdown on drugs was hailed in the main conference hall before being blown up by a new generation of more liberal Tories admitting they had taken illegal substances as students. In his tribute, Andrew Rosindell MP said Ann was not the sort of politician who needed an autocue (though, having briefed her on social security policy at the time of 2001 general election, I know for a fact that she did her homework diligently before speaking her mind).

All party conferences are bubbles. But this one is more bubble-like than most. (Few people there have been talking about the Channel 4 exposé even if it was by far and away the one part of the Reform UK conference that the world outside were looking at.) Yet it is a bubble that the higher education sector has finally found its way inside.

* The first gig I ever attended, back in 1987, was Suzanne Vega at Birmingham’s NEC, the venue for Reform UK’s Annual Conference. Her setlist included ‘Left of Center’, so I’ve pinched my title from her. But there were more pyrotechnics at the Reform event than the pop concert.

title: WEEKEND READING: What if English universities itemised tuition fees like US universities?

The post WEEKEND READING: What if English universities itemised tuition fees like US universities? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join the Policy Institute at King’s College London and HEPI on Tuesday 15 September, from 6.30pm to 7.45pm, at Bush House, London, for a free event exploring the future of higher education in England. Drawing on Professor Sir Chris Husbands’ report, New choices: Revisiting futures for higher education in England, the discussion will consider how financial pressures, generative AI, changing student expectations and declining public trust are reshaping the sector – and the choices universities and government need to make now to secure a sustainable future. Register here.

This blog was kindly authored by Vincenzo Raimo and Jamie Warner, both independent higher education consultants.

We recently came across a LinkedIn post from the father of a student about to begin his studies at Virginia Tech in the United States. He had shared his son’s tuition fee statement, which itemised not just tuition itself but a whole range of compulsory charges for technology, student health, library access, sports and student activities, student services, and even a separate orientation fee.

It made us wonder what an equivalent fee statement might look like for students at an English university. Not because we think we should necessarily adopt the American approach but because increasingly students and parents are asking: what exactly are we paying for?

A little over a decade ago, when the undergraduate tuition fee in England increased to £9,000, many universities published attractive infographics showing how that money was spent. They typically divided the fee between headings such as teaching, libraries, student support, estates and administration. The intention was to demonstrate value for money and reassure students that their fees were being spent on their education.

Those graphics undoubtedly served a purpose, but they also told only part of the story.

For one thing, they often implied that tuition fees were spent directly on the individual student. In reality, universities are complex organisations with multiple income streams including research funding, international tuition fees, commercial activities, philanthropy and investment income. Tuition fees become part of a much larger pool of funding rather than being ring-fenced for individual students or courses.

More importantly, they rarely acknowledged some of the characteristics that define a modern, comprehensive university

Academic staff don’t simply teach. They also undertake research, scholarship, curriculum development, knowledge exchange, enterprise, public engagement and academic leadership. Universities maintain laboratories, libraries, museums, archives, specialist collections and research facilities that enrich the learning environment but are difficult to allocate neatly under a heading such as teaching. Nor did those graphics usually recognise the cost of servicing the borrowing used to finance new buildings and major infrastructure projects, or investing in the next generation of digital and physical learning spaces. Whether or not one agrees with those investment decisions, they are now a significant part of the economics of running many modern universities.

Perhaps that is one reason why most of those ‘where your tuition fee goes’ graphics have quietly disappeared.

There is another interesting aspect to this discussion. Whether in Virginia or in Nottingham, students inevitably contribute towards facilities and services they may never personally use. A History student helps support laboratories. An Engineering student contributes towards libraries and archives they may rarely visit. Many students never use the sports centre but contribute to its upkeep. Equally, research-active academics may spend part of their time creating knowledge rather than standing in front of a lecture theatre.

That is not a flaw in the system. It is simply part of belonging to a university rather than purchasing a series of individual services. Indeed, one of the distinguishing characteristics of a comprehensive university is that students benefit from being part of a much broader academic community than their own degree programme alone. They study alongside students from other disciplines, learn from research-active academics, and have access to a wider range of facilities, expertise and opportunities than they may ever use personally. Those shared resources are part of the educational experience, even if no individual student makes use of all of them.

Now imagine how the current maximum regulated undergraduate tuition fee in England (£9,535) might be presented.

To make this thought experiment more realistic, we have based the illustrative figures on the latest available HESA Finance data for 2024–25 together with the Office for Students’ 2023-24 analysis of sector-wide TRAC cost recovery rates. HESA groups university expenditure into broad accounting categories; we have translated those into language that we hope is more meaningful for students while retaining the same underlying pattern of expenditure.

The figures represent sector averages rather than the finances of any individual university or course, applying the 89.2% TRAC recovery rate for home students reported in OfS’s 2023–24 analysis. They should not be interpreted as the cost or financial performance of any individual course, and cross-subsidy between subjects, courses and activities is a longstanding feature of the university funding model.

Annual Undergraduate Tuition Fee Statement, along with university contribution (illustrative): £9,535

Now imagine the same approach for an international undergraduate paying, say, £24,000 per year. The same methodology is applied to the international undergraduate example, using a full economic cost recovery rate of 143.1%. This produces the reverse position: the illustrative fee exceeds the estimated cost of provision. Rather than presenting the difference as a ‘negative subsidy’, we describe it as an investment in educational quality and the wider university community, reflecting the contribution international fee income makes to research, specialist provision, facilities and the broader institutional mission.

Annual International Undergraduate Tuition Fee Statement (illustrative): £24,000

The final category is perhaps the most interesting – though, again, the £7,229 figure attached to it here is a sector-wide average, not a claim about any actual university’s accounts. Cross-subsidy has long been part of the economics of higher education. International tuition fees do not simply fund the education of international students. They also help sustain research, expensive disciplines, specialist facilities, widening participation, civic engagement and future investment. Equally, domestic tuition fees contribute towards maintaining the wider academic environment from which all students benefit, even if those benefits are not always visible on a timetable or in a module handbook.

Perhaps universities have sometimes been reluctant to explain this explicitly to their current and future students.

The Virginia Tech statement itemises the cost of higher education, while English universities have traditionally presented tuition as a single, all-inclusive fee. Yet, in both cases, students are contributing to much more than the individual services they personally use. They are helping to sustain an academic community that combines teaching, research, specialist facilities and a wide range of shared resources.

It is almost the opposite of the medieval University of Bologna, where students effectively hired individual scholars to teach them. Today’s universities are far more complex institutions. Students are not simply buying lectures; they are joining an academic community that combines teaching, research, innovation, culture and public engagement. Their tuition fee helps sustain that wider ecosystem.

We are not suggesting English universities should copy the American approach. But the exercise has been revealing. Attempting to explain what the tuition fee supports quickly demonstrates just how difficult it is to separate teaching from research, libraries from laboratories, or individual students from the wider academic community. Perhaps that complexity is precisely what makes a university a university.

Perhaps the question should not simply be: where does my tuition fee go? But rather: what kind of university does my tuition fee help to create?

title: IDP to consolidate 15 India student placement locations
summary:
Around 200 employees are understood to be affected as the international education company responds to falling student volumes and shifting visa policies across major study destinations.

The post IDP to consolidate 15 India student placement locations appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
IDP Education will consolidate 15 student placement locations across India into larger nearby offices, with around 200 employees understood to be affected by the changes.

The company confirmed the consolidation to The PIE News following a review of its Indian network, citing changing student demand and evolving visa and market conditions across key destination countries.

“Following a review of our student placement network in India, IDP has made the decision to consolidate 15 locations into nearby, larger IDP offices that are well positioned to continue supporting students and partners in those markets,” an IDP spokesperson said.

“The changes reflect evolving student placement demand in certain locations, as well as our continued focus on high-quality student recruitment, strong student outcomes and an effective service model.”

IDP did not confirm the number of affected employees or disclose which locations would be consolidated or when the changes would take effect.

Following the changes, IDP will retain 52 offices across India, where it established its first office more than 30 years ago.

IDP said affected students had been proactively informed and would continue to receive counselling and other support through their nearest office and its wider service network.

“Our priority throughout the transition is to maintain continuity of service and the high standards expected by students and partner institutions,” the spokesperson said.

The company provided no details about potential redundancies or redeployment.

“We are also supporting our people through this transition and thank impacted colleagues for their professionalism, contribution and commitment to IDP,” the spokesperson said.

The announcement follows two difficult financial years for IDP, as tighter immigration policies across Australia, Canada, the UK and the US have weighed on global student mobility.

IDP reported a 9% fall in revenue to AUD $795.4 million in FY26, while student placement volumes declined by 27% and English language testing volumes fell by 8%. Language teaching volumes increased by 1%.

The company cut around 1,250 roles, equivalent to 20% of its workforce, during the year and reduced its global IELTS testing network from approximately 1,500 venues to fewer than 600.

IDP achieved AUD $32m in cost reductions during FY26, exceeding its AUD $25m target, and plans to reduce costs by a further AUD $15m in FY27. Its outlook for the current financial year assumes market volumes will be 20%–30% lower than in FY26.

“Our focus this year has been to manage financial performance whilst progressing the multi-year transformation program to reduce cost, simplify the business and position for future growth,” IDP chief executive and managing director Tennealle O’Shannessy said when the results were released in August.

We remain deeply committed to India and to working closely with our university and institution partners to navigate changing market conditions, maintain high standards of student recruitment and build sustainable growth together

IDP spokesperson

The FY26 decline followed an already challenging year for the company. Revenue fell by 15% to AUD $882.2m in FY25, while gross profit dropped by 21% to AUD $525.8m and global university placement volumes decreased by 29%.

Placement volumes fell in Canada, Australia, the UK and the US that year, declining by 56%, 22%, 18% and 25%, respectively. By contrast, placements increased by 40% in New Zealand and 37% in Ireland.

The downturn was particularly pronounced in India, where IELTS volumes fell by 50% in FY25 after declining by 42% the previous year. IDP’s earnings across Asia also dropped by 40%, with the company citing its Indian operations among several factors affecting the result.

IDP is one of the three co-owners of IELTS and has delivered all IELTS tests in India since acquiring the British Council’s local testing operations for £130m in 2021. Its Indian business includes both English language testing and student placement services.

The company began implementing cost reductions in 2024 after forecasting that the international education market would contract by 20%–25% amid tighter policies in leading destination countries. At the time, IDP said the programme was not expected to affect its operating footprint.

It has since launched what it describes as a multi-year transformation aimed at simplifying the business, reducing costs and adopting a more agile, AI-enabled operating model. IDP has also said it is investing in technology and AI-supported counselling.

The company’s operational changes have extended beyond India. In July 2026, IDP outsourced its onshore visa-support services in Australia to Bravo Migration, replacing its in-house registered migration agents.

Separately, IDP expanded its placement portfolio into Malaysia and the UAE in 2026, citing changing student preferences and demand for alternatives to major English-speaking destinations.

Despite the consolidation, IDP said India remained one of its most important source markets and was central to its long-term growth ambitions.

“We remain deeply committed to India and to working closely with our university and institution partners to navigate changing market conditions, maintain high standards of student recruitment and build sustainable growth together,” the spokesperson said.

title: The PIEoneer Awards 2026: winners revealed
summary:
Innovation and achievement across the international education sector has once again been recognised at The PIEoneer Awards ceremony, now in its 10th year.

The post The PIEoneer Awards 2026: winners revealed appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Winners across 21 categories were announced at a glamorous event hosted at the historic Guildhall in London. Meanwhile, many more entrants were recognised as highly commended for their outstanding achievements and contributions to global education over the past year.

Last night’s celebrations were particularly special, marking a decade of The PIEoneer Awards. For the 10th year in a row, finalists showed innovation, determination and a truly global outlook in the face of mounting challenges facing the global international education sector.

“Even after 10 years of The PIEoneer Awards, we continue to be blown away with the exceptional quality of entrants. Our winners have demonstrated a real commitment to making a difference, and we’re thrilled to recognise their achievements,” commented The PIE’s COO and co-founder, Clare Gossage.

International education is a sector that never stands still, and this year’s winners are testament to the people continually pushing it forward

Clare Gossage, The PIE

“International education is a sector that never stands still, and this year’s winners are testament to the people continually pushing it forward. From pioneering new approaches to championing inclusion and creating meaningful opportunities, they represent the very best of our industry.”

A distinguished judging panel – representing a wide range of expertise and international backgrounds – sought out individuals and organisations redefining excellence and driving progress in global education.

This year, the flagship PIEoneer of the year award recognised US-based Technovation for its project-based learning philosophy where students build real technology solutions to community challenges.

Each year, The PIE recognises an individual for their Outstanding contribution to the industry, with Oxford International Education Group (OIEG) CEO Lil Bremermann-Richard taking home the coveted trophy last night for her boundary-pushing career spanning over two decades as a leading figure in international education.

title: The student loan scam looking to dupe already anxious students
summary:
Scammers hope to siphon off some of the £2.6bn in student maintenance funds paid out each September

You are about to start university and can’t wait but then you receive a worrying text message. It is a few days before the first student loan payment is due to land in your account and apparently someone has tried to alter your bank details.

“Our records indicate that your bank details on your student finance account were changed on Friday 16th. If you did not do this please contact us immediately,” says the text.

full_text:
You are about to start university and can’t wait but then you receive a worrying text message. It is a few days before the first student loan payment is due to land in your account and apparently someone has tried to alter your bank details.

“Our records indicate that your bank details on your student finance account were changed on Friday 16th. If you did not do this please contact us immediately,” says the text.

You click on the web link in the message and go to what you think is the website of the Students Loans Company (SLC), the government body that administers loans and grants. You log in to check that everything is OK, put in your bank details and the screen says: “Thanks for confirming.” But what you have done is supply this important information to criminals.

Acting quickly, the scammers then use your log-in details to access your real account and change the bank account so that your student loan payment is diverted to them.

The government is making a fresh push to raise awareness of this fraud as the new academic year starts.

This month, about £2.6bn is being paid out in maintenance support to 1.1 million students. The first of three loan payments will be deposited in the accounts of students in England and Wales. Students from Northern Ireland and Scotland get their loan instalments every month.

In the last academic year, £519,000 was lost to scammers who defrauded 168 students, according to the SLC. More than 1,100 people had their details changed but in most cases the fraud was stopped before money was lost.

What the scam looks like

Scammers are using several methods including text message, email or phone calls to target students.

The messages can claim that a payment is at risk because bank details need to be updated. Or it may say that an account has been closed unless the student acts immediately to log in to their “account” through the link provided.

The link supplied in the message leads to a clone of the SLC site and students are asked to input their details.

“It’s a race against time because the criminals then use those details to log into our genuine site to change the bank account on the genuine student account to divert the maintenance loan payment before we spot it,” said Alan Balanowski, the risk director at SLC.

Criminals know that billions of pounds will land in students’ accounts this month and have timed their approach to coordinate the fraud with a sense of urgency that people may not get their money when they need it. This is a common tactic used by criminals to get people to act in haste.

What to do

Be aware of when you could be the target of scams – September, January and April are the months when the student loan instalments are paid in England and Wales.

SLC says it won’t ask you to confirm personal or financial information by email, text or on social media. Don’t click on any links provided, instead log in to your account through the Gov.uk website.

Students are also urged to not publicise when they are getting their payment by refraining from putting it on social media.

SLC says that it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media. So immediately be suspicious if you are contacted in either of these ways.

Any fraudulent emails can be sent on to report@phishing.gov.uk while scam text messages can be forwarded to 7726.

If you suspect your account has been compromised, change the password immediately and contact SLC. Victims should be able to get a replacement payment so there is no financial loss to them.

title: Al congresso mondiale Cibjo focus su sostenibilità e fiducia degli acquirenti
summary: L’industria dei preziosi a convegno in Italia elabora nuove strategie per superare le difficoltà attuali
full_text:
È necessario rafforzare la fiducia degli acquirenti nel mercato dei preziosi, messa a rischio dalla confusione creata sul mercato dal marketing spesso aggressivo dei diamanti sintetici (sempre meno chiamati laboratory grown). E bisogna tenere la barra dritta sulla sostenibilità, necessaria per frenare i cambiamenti climatici in atto e mitigare le diseguaglianze che incrinano la coesione sociale. Ma le strategie di sostenibilità devono essere più pragmatiche e meno ideologiche, procedurali e normative perché scontiamo un eccesso di regole inattuabili. Solo così si supererà la crisi in atto nel settore dei diamanti e il rallentamento del mercato dei gioielli, aumentando la resilienza del comparto per resistere alle fluttazioni del prezzo dell’oro, che tanti problemi hanno creato.

Chiedilo al Sole

sulla base del contenuto visualizzato.

Sono questi i temi principali trattati al congresso mondiale di Cibjo-The world jewellery confederation, inaugurato ieri all’interno della fiera Vicenzaoro, ospite di Italian exhibition group (Ieg). «Festeggiamo il centenario della confederazione internazionale proprio in Italia per riconoscerne l’eccellenza mondiale della manifattura e del design - ha detto il presidente Gaetano Cavalieri -. I 600 delegati da 40 Paesi di tutti i continenti stanno riflettendo assieme su come superare il momento di rallentamento attuale della domanda e di riduzione dei margini. Vedremo diversi cambi di strategia in arrivo, perché questa industria è sana, reattiva e vuole costruire il mercato per prosperare anche nei prossimi cento anni e continuare a mantenere 120 milioni di persone in tutto il mondo, dalle miniere alle gioiellerie, dalle manifatture alle borse dei preziosi, fino alle fiere come Vicenzaoro».

Sarebbe troppo facile, però, fare salire diamanti e criteri Esg (environmental, social, governance) sul banco degli imputati come unici responsabili della difficile congiuntura. Ma tutti i rappresentanti della filiera dei diamanti presenti hanno pronunciato con onestà la parola tabù al congresso dell’anno scorso: crisi. Ne ha parlato apertamente anche Gareth Penny, a capo della cordata pre-selezionata da Anglo American e dal Governo del Botswana come acquirente (preferred bidder) di De Beers. «Supereremo la crisi del settore dei diamanti partendo dalla riscossa del colosso De Beers - ha detto -. Una riscossa che deve essere basata sul marketing emozionale, sulla promessa di amore che un anello di diamante trasmette. Bisogna capire che il settore non vende chimica, ma emozioni. Del resto, fu De Beers a creare la domanda di diamanti cent’anni fa con un marketing molto indovinato; e ora la stessa società può e deve aiutare a riaccendere la passione degli acquirenti e aiutare tutto il settore a ripartire. Ma bisogna lavorare in modo strategico per recuperare posizioni, perché ad esempio ora ben metà del mercato Usa degli anelli di fidanzamento è diventato appannaggio dei diamanti sintetici, a discapito di quelli naturali».

I rappresentanti di tutte le filiere a congresso (in primis pietre preziose, oro, platino, gioielli) hanno apprezzato, non a caso, i lavori della commissione diamanti di Cibjo, che sta riscrivendo le definizioni e le regole per aggiornare il Blue book usato anche a livello legale. Altre novità sono in arrivo sulla definizione di giada preziosa, un mercato secondo solo a quello dei diamanti, ma su cui la confusione mina la fiducia degli acquirenti.

I lavori del congresso Cibjo continueranno fino a lunedì 7 settembre. E c’è da scommettere che i delegati continueranno a discutere sui concetti di rinnovo della fiducia dei consumatori, sulla nuova definizione di diamanti sintetici e non più di lab grown e su nuove strategie di marketing e “sostenibilità sostenibile”.
